answers.product: It's a software factory repo, for developers who want to have a sensible software factory from the get-go. Rather than treating every project as a bespoke effort, a software factory applies manufacturing-style repeatability to software delivery: templates, shared platforms, automated builds and tests, security controls, and deployment pipelines. The result is faster, more consistent delivery with fewer manual handoffs. It's a bit opinionated in the fact that it is built on Cloudflare, but it's a good way to get a SaaS off the ground running. Name: not really fixed. Generally it's a software factory, but what we have is more like a cf-saas-software-factory starter (I'm not affiliated with Cloudflare). What hurts today: right now people are just vibe coding, and/or don't know how to make their own software factory because the effort is ginormous on its own. What they use now: people are manually using skills and plugins and have to create their own environment; vibe coders wouldn't know how to do this. They may be using Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one (also a set from a Y Combinator founder whose name the founder forgot).
answers.persona: Aimed at solo developers, startups, or people trying to create a framework inside their agency. Asked to pick one primary user, the founder said: I want to build for solo developer, startup team and agency lead. They want a software factory that they can start from. What stops them: right now they have nothing to build on top of. Others who may use it as a starting point: developers, vibe coders, product and UI/UX people who want something solid, or even new developers. There is no auth system, so nobody signs up. Who it is not for: not sure yet.
answers.scenario: Someone starting a SaaS, and they need the latest and greatest tools and workflows to get started. They scour through whatever GitHub links they can find and have to invoke each skill manually, making themselves a bottleneck rather than a software factory. How often: every time they have an app idea. Done looks like: they initialize their own factory and get to work. Where they are and on what device: not said.
answers.alsoAffected: Mostly teammates, on the DX side of things, then users of the said SaaS product. What each should feel: nothing separate was given; the founder gave only the product's overall feel.
answers.feel: The product should feel: simple, composable and succinct. It must never feel: complex, bloated, too much.
answers.goals: Three months (by 27 February 2027): 50 GitHub stars, people start using this, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users. One year (by 27 November 2027): 1000 GitHub stars and 3 examples; hopefully we get traction and people start using this as a framework just like shadcn, where they can plug and play features.
answers.earns: Free and open source. The return: it speeds up our client work. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.
answers.antiGoals: Custom skills and custom plugins: we should be shipping workflows, not skills and plugins. We're not making anything new but creating a factory of how the skills and plugins work together. It's okay when skills are bundled with the workflow. Building outside Cloudflare: Cloudflare has the most amazing DX, as you can add services via wrangler and test it locally with the same API. Keeping true as a software factory.
answers.assumptions: People want a whole factory, not single skills.

# Product foundation

## Product
A software factory starter built on Cloudflare, for solo developers who want a sensible factory from the start instead of treating each project as bespoke work; the name is a working name ("software factory", or closer, "cf-saas-software-factory starter"), and the founder is not affiliated with Cloudflare.

## Problem
People vibe code, or cannot build their own software factory because the effort is ginormous. Today they invoke skills and plugins by hand and build their own environment. They use Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one, including a set from a Y Combinator founder. They have nothing to build on top of, so each person becomes the bottleneck instead of a factory. Why leave single skills: an agency needs one shared setup.

## Persona
Solo developer. Alone, at a laptop, with a new idea. Wants a software factory to start from. What stops them: they have nothing to build on top of.

## Core scenario
A solo developer has an app idea and starts a SaaS, every time they have one. They need the latest and greatest tools and workflows. Today they search GitHub links and invoke each skill by hand. Done: they initialize their own factory and get to work.

## Also affected
Startup teams and agency leads, who also want a factory to start from. Teammates, on the developer experience side. Then users of the SaaS products built this way. See Open.

## Not for
Anyone not on Cloudflare.

## Feel
Simple, composable, succinct. Never complex, bloated or too much.

## Goals
1. By 27 February 2027: 50 GitHub stars.
2. By 27 February 2027: 5 outside repos using it, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users.
3. By 27 November 2027: 1000 GitHub stars, and 3 examples of ours plus 5 from outsiders. Hope for traction, with people using it as a framework like shadcn, plugging in features.

Earns by: free and open source; the return is faster client work for us, meaning fewer bugs and more production-ready work instead of AI slop. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.

## Anti-goals
1. Custom skills and custom plugins. We ship workflows, not skills and plugins. We make nothing new; we build a factory for how existing skills and plugins work together. A skill bundled with a workflow is fine if it is useless outside that workflow.
2. Building on any host but Cloudflare. Cloudflare has the best developer experience: add services via wrangler and test locally with the same API. This keeps it a true software factory. Non-Cloudflare services such as Stripe are allowed; only other hosts are banned.
3. A hosted or paid version of the factory (a platform, dashboard or SaaS). Never. See Open.

## Assumptions
- People want a whole factory, not single skills. Not proven.
- Others share the problem. So far the evidence is the founder's own repeated pain.

## Open
- Product: the name is not fixed.
- Problem: the Y Combinator founder's skill set is unnamed; the founder forgot the name.
- Persona: developers, vibe coders, product and UI/UX people and new developers may use it as a starting point; whether they are users is not said. Problem names vibe coders as unable to build a factory themselves.
- Persona: the solo developer is primary, but the reason given to leave single skills is that an agency needs one shared setup; the two pull against each other.
- Also affected: what teammates and SaaS users should feel is not said; only the product's overall feel was given.
- Goals: 5 outside repos by February 2027 and 5 outsider examples by November 2027 are the same number nine months apart, and 2 to 3 examples of ours against 3 barely differ; one target may be too low.
- Goals: no number is set for donations, and "fewer bugs, more production ready" has no measure.
- Anti-goals: no reason is given for never building a hosted product.
- Assumptions: no test is set for whether people want a whole factory.

# Product foundation

## Product
A software factory starter built on Cloudflare, for solo developers who want a sensible factory from the start instead of treating each project as bespoke work; the name is a working name ("software factory", or closer, "cf-saas-software-factory starter"), and the founder is not affiliated with Cloudflare.

## Problem
People vibe code, or cannot build their own software factory because the effort is ginormous. Today they invoke skills and plugins by hand and build their own environment. They use Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one, including a set from a Y Combinator founder. At a new idea they start blank, use create-t3-app, start from a template, or copy a set of skills. They have nothing to build on top of, so each person becomes the bottleneck instead of a factory. The factory is proven and eval'd to give high quality, predictable designs and code.

## Persona
Solo developer. Alone, at a laptop, with a new idea, building their own SaaS ideas and client work for others. Wants a software factory to start from: set up once, reuse every idea. What stops them: they have nothing to build on top of.

## Core scenario
A solo developer has an app idea and starts a SaaS, every time they have one. They need the latest and greatest tools and workflows. Today they search GitHub links and invoke each skill by hand. Done: they initialize their own factory and get to work.

## Also affected
Teammates, on the developer experience side: they should find it clear. Users of the SaaS products built this way: they should find them polished. Startup teams and agency leads also want a factory to start from; team features such as multi-user permissions or shared agency config are deferred past February 2027.

## Not for
Anyone not on Cloudflare. A developer with no Cloudflare account yet is fine.

## Feel
Simple, composable, succinct. Never complex, bloated or too much.

## Goals
1. By 27 February 2027: 150 GitHub stars.
2. By 27 February 2027: 5 outside repos using it, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users.
3. By 27 February 2027: 3 of our own client projects start from the factory.
4. By 27 November 2027: 1000 GitHub stars, and 3 examples of ours plus 5 from outsiders. Hope for traction, with people using it as a framework like shadcn, plugging in features.

Earns by: free and open source; the return is faster client work for us, meaning fewer bugs and more production-ready work instead of AI slop. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.

## Anti-goals
1. Custom skills and custom plugins. We ship workflows, not skills and plugins. We make nothing new; we build a factory for how existing skills and plugins work together. A skill bundled with a workflow is fine if it is useless outside that workflow.
2. Building on any host but Cloudflare. Cloudflare has the best developer experience: add services via wrangler and test locally with the same API. This keeps it a true software factory. Non-Cloudflare services such as Stripe are allowed; only other hosts are banned.
3. A hosted or paid version of the factory (a platform, dashboard or SaaS), and all paid offers. Never. Hosted docs only are fine.

## Assumptions
- People want a whole factory, not single skills. Not proven.
- Others share the problem. So far the evidence is the founder's own repeated pain.

## Open
- Product: the name is not fixed.
- Problem: the Y Combinator founder's skill set is unnamed; the founder forgot the name.
- Problem: vibe coders are named as unable to build a factory themselves, but whether they are users is not said.
- Goals: no stop point is set for February 2027; nothing says what result means change course.
- Goals: "fewer bugs, more production ready" has no measure.
- Goals: no number is set for donations, and a donation page pulls against the ban on all paid offers.
- Goals: outside repos are counted by asking the community or private testers; no exact method or proof is set.
- Goals: 5 outside repos by February 2027 and 5 outsider examples by November 2027 are the same number nine months apart, and 2 to 3 examples of ours against 3 barely differ; one target may be too low. It is not said if an outside repo and an outsider example are the same.

questions.question: Does the solo developer write and review the code themselves, or mostly direct an AI to write it (vibe coding)?
questions.why: The Problem names vibe coders but never says if they are users, so two readers picture a different person at the laptop.

questions.question: Is the moment you write for the first-time setup of the factory, or starting each new idea from a factory already set up?
questions.why: The scenario says "every time they have one" yet ends with "they initialize their own factory", so readers picture different moments and different Done states.
options: Both, setup is the first idea

questions.question: Should Not for also turn away developers who want a different framework or language than the one the template is built on?
questions.why: Not for names only Cloudflare, so a Next.js or non-TypeScript developer on Cloudflare would sign up and then find the factory is not for them.
options: Stack fixed; not in Not for

questions.question: Does a donation page such as Buy Me a Coffee stay in, given anti-goal 3 rules out all paid offers?
questions.why: The earning line allows a donation page while the anti-goal bans every paid offer, so one of the two must change or gain an exception.

questions.question: Are the 3 client projects in goal 3 the same as the 2 to 3 SaaS examples of ours in goal 2?
questions.why: If they are the same, goal 2 and the 'ours' count in goal 4 double-count one set of projects and the real target is lower than it reads.

questions.question: Is a managed data service outside Cloudflare, such as Neon, Supabase or Turso, allowed like Stripe, or does it count as another host?
questions.why: Anti-goal 2 bans other hosts but allows services, and a database that holds the app's data is the most tempting case on that line.

questions.question: Does the ban on all paid offers also cover a donation page such as Buy Me a Coffee?
questions.why: Earns by and Anti-goals now contradict each other, so a feature like a sponsor badge cannot be judged until one wins.

questions.question: Should the factory refuse to run a hosted registry of community features, as shadcn does, given Goal 4 hopes for people plugging in features?
questions.why: A hosted registry is the obvious step toward Goal 4 but may break the ban on a hosted version.

questions.question: Besides yourself, who have you seen or heard hit this problem, and would any of them say they would switch?
questions.why: The only evidence is the founder's own pain, so the document cannot yet say the problem is real for others, and a few named people would change Problem and Assumptions.

questions.question: Which of your repeated pains is the worst: a bespoke setup per idea, inconsistent code quality, or time lost choosing tools?
questions.why: The Problem lists several pains, and naming the worst tells readers what the factory must fix first and what would make someone leave create-t3-app.

questions.question: If people want single skills or a plain template and not a whole factory, would you still build this for your own client work?
questions.why: This decides whether the whole-factory assumption ends the product or only ends the outside-adoption goals.
options: Yes, it pays off for us alone
Unsure, decide at a set date
